questions.q: State the classical definition of oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen transfer.
questions.a: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. A wrong answer (e.g., "oxidation is loss of oxygen") reveals the student has memorised the terms backwards — a very common error that leads to misidentifying oxidised/reduced species in every subsequent question.

questions.q: In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, explain why Fe₂O₃ is said to be reduced and CO is oxidised, using the classical definition.
questions.a: Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen (loss of oxygen = reduction) to form Fe; CO gains oxygen (gain of oxygen = oxidation) to form CO₂. A wrong answer (e.g., "Fe₂O₃ gains oxygen") shows the student cannot track oxygen atoms across reactants and products — they look only at the formula Fe₂O₃ and see oxygen present, missing that it decreases from 3 O atoms per formula unit to zero in Fe.

questions.q: Identify the oxidised and reduced species in the reaction: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Use the electronic definition (electron transfer).
questions.a: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation, loss of electrons); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction, gain of electrons). Zn is oxidised (reducing agent), Cu²⁺ is reduced (oxidising agent). A wrong answer (e.g., "Cu is oxidised because it becomes Cu²⁺") reveals the student confuses the elemental form with the ion — they see Cu on the product side and think it lost electrons, not recognising Cu²⁺ on the reactant side gained electrons to become Cu.

questions.q: Compare the two reactions: (i) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO and (ii) H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. In which reaction does oxidation occur according to the classical definition? In which does it occur according to the electronic definition? Explain any difference.
questions.a: Classical: Reaction (i) — Mg gains oxygen (oxidation); Reaction (ii) — no oxygen/hydrogen transfer, so classical definition does not apply. Electronic: Both reactions — Mg loses electrons (oxidation) in (i); H₂ loses electrons (oxidation) in (ii). A wrong answer (e.g., "only reaction (i) shows oxidation") shows the student thinks oxidation requires oxygen — they haven't internalised that the electronic definition extends the concept beyond oxygen-containing reactions.

questions.q: A student writes: "In the reaction MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O, MnO₂ is the reducing agent because it loses oxygen." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. MnO₂ loses oxygen (reduction), so it is the oxidising agent (it causes HCl to be oxidised). HCl loses electrons (Cl⁻ → Cl₂) and is the reducing agent. A wrong evaluation (e.g., agreeing with the student) reveals the classic confusion: the substance that is reduced is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent. Students mix up "agent" with "process" — the agent is the reactant that causes the other species to undergo that process.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using iron nails and copper sulphate solution to demonstrate oxidation and reduction. State what you would observe and which species is oxidised/reduced.
questions.a: Place an iron nail in blue CuSO₄ solution. Observe: blue colour fades (Cu²⁺ reduced to Cu), reddish-brown deposit forms on nail (Cu), solution turns pale green (Fe²⁺ formed). Reaction: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu. Fe is oxidised (loses 2e⁻), Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains 2e⁻). A poor answer (e.g., "iron rusts") shows the student cannot connect displacement reactions (c10_chem_cbse_01_005) to redox — they see only a colour change, not electron transfer.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance, or the loss of electrons by an atom/ion; reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance, or the gain of electrons by an atom/ion.
Fill in the blank: Begin with a real-world observation: an iron nail left in the rain develops a ______-brown coating (rust), while a copper vessel turns green over time.
What is Oxidation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance, or the loss of electrons by an atom/ion; reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance, or the gain of electrons by an atom/ion.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Oxidation?
questions.a: Students consistently confuse the oxidising agent with the species that is oxidised.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced in a given chemical equation using both the classical (oxygen/hydrogen transfer) and electronic (electron transfer) definitions, and can name the oxidising and reducing agents.
